questions.q: Heat transfer through a vacuum can only occur by:
questions.solution:
**Radiation** — infrared electromagnetic waves, which need no medium at all.

That is how the Sun's energy crosses $150$ million km of empty space. Conduction needs particles in contact; convection needs a fluid to circulate.

questions.q: Metals are good conductors of heat because they contain:
questions.solution:
**Free (delocalised) electrons** move rapidly through the metal, carrying energy from the hot end to the cold far faster than vibration alone could.

Non-metals have no free electrons and must rely on vibrations passing from atom to atom, which is why they are poor conductors.

questions.q: In a transverse wave, the particles vibrate:
questions.solution:
**Perpendicular** to the direction the wave travels — water waves, light, and a wave on a rope.

In a **longitudinal** wave, such as sound, the particles vibrate **along** the direction of travel, making compressions and rarefactions.
options: perpendicular to the direction of travel

questions.solution:
$\mathbf{v = f\lambda}$ — speed equals frequency times wavelength.

In a given medium the speed is fixed, so a higher frequency must mean a shorter wavelength. The two are inversely related.

questions.q: When a wave is reflected, the angle of incidence is:
questions.solution:
$\angle i = \angle r$, both measured **from the normal**.

It holds for light, sound, water waves — every kind of wave.
options: greater than the angle of reflection
less than the angle of reflection
equal to the angle of reflection

questions.q: A wave has frequency $50$ Hz and wavelength $4$ m. Find its speed, in m/s.
A wave has a period of $0.02$ s. Find its frequency, in Hz.
questions.solution:
$f = \dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{1}{0.02} = \mathbf{50}$ Hz.

Frequency and period are reciprocals: one counts waves per second, the other seconds per wave.

questions.q: An echo returns after $3$ s from a cliff $510$ m away. Find the speed of sound, in m/s.
questions.solution:
The sound travels **there and back**: $2 \times 510 = 1020$ m.

$v = \dfrac{1020}{3} = \mathbf{340}$ m/s.

Forgetting to double the distance is the standard error in every echo question.

questions.q: Light of speed $3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s has frequency $5 \times 10^{14}$ Hz. Find its wavelength in nm.
Light slows from $3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s to $2 \times 10^{8}$ m/s entering glass. Find the refractive index.
Describe conduction, convection and radiation, and explain how a vacuum flask reduces all three.
questions.solution:
**Conduction.** Energy passes through a solid as vibrating particles jostle their neighbours, and in metals also by **free electrons**. It needs particles in contact, so it does not happen in a vacuum.

**Convection.** Warm fluid expands, becomes less dense, and **rises**; cooler fluid sinks to take its place, setting up a **convection current**. It happens only in liquids and gases, since it needs the material itself to move.

**Radiation.** Infrared waves, emitted by every object above absolute zero. **No medium is needed**, and dark matt surfaces emit and absorb best while shiny silvered ones reflect.

**The vacuum flask — each feature defeats one mechanism:**

1. **The vacuum between the double walls** stops **conduction and convection** entirely: no particles, no transfer.

2. **Silvered surfaces** on both sides of the vacuum **reflect radiation** back the way it came.

3. **The stopper** stops convection and **evaporation** through the top — the biggest loss of all from a hot drink.

4. **The plastic case and supports** are poor conductors, minimising the small leak through the flask's neck.

It is the clearest example in the syllabus of a design answering a physical analysis point by point — and the same flask keeps cold drinks cold, because it blocks heat travelling in either direction.

questions.q: Compare transverse and longitudinal waves, define wavelength, frequency, amplitude and period, and state the wave equation.
questions.solution:
**Transverse waves** — particles vibrate **perpendicular** to the direction of travel.

*Examples:* light and all electromagnetic waves, water waves, waves on a rope, S-waves in an earthquake.

They have crests and troughs, and **can be polarised**.

**Longitudinal waves** — particles vibrate **along** the direction of travel.

*Examples:* sound, P-waves in an earthquake.

They have compressions and rarefactions, **cannot be polarised**, and cannot travel through a vacuum, since they need particles to compress.

**The quantities.**

• **Wavelength ($\lambda$)** — the distance between two consecutive identical points, in metres.

• **Frequency ($f$)** — waves passing a point per second, in hertz.

• **Amplitude** — the maximum displacement from the rest position. It determines **loudness** for sound and **brightness** for light.

• **Period ($T$)** — the time for one complete wave, $T = \dfrac{1}{f}$.

**Wave equation:** $\mathbf{v = f\lambda}$.

**Note what a wave carries.** Energy travels along a wave, but the particles themselves only vibrate about a fixed position — a cork on water bobs up and down while the wave moves past it.

questions.q: State the laws of reflection and refraction, explain total internal reflection, and give two applications.
questions.solution:
**Laws of reflection.**

1. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the **normal**.

2. The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal lie in the same plane.

**Refraction.** Light changes speed on entering a new medium and therefore bends.

• Into a **denser** medium (air $\to$ glass): slows down, bends **towards** the normal.

• Into a **less dense** medium (glass $\to$ air): speeds up, bends **away** from the normal.

**Snell's law:** $n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$.

**Total internal reflection.** Going from dense to less dense, the refracted ray bends further from the normal as the angle of incidence grows. At the **critical angle** it grazes along the boundary at $90°$.

Beyond that angle, **no light escapes at all** — it is entirely reflected back inside.

**Two conditions:** dense to less dense, and the angle of incidence greater than the critical angle. $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{n}$, which gives about $42°$ for glass.

**Applications.**

1. **Optical fibres** — light bounces along the core for kilometres with almost no loss, carrying telephone and internet traffic, and images in an endoscope.

2. **Prisms in binoculars and periscopes**, which give a brighter image than mirrors because **nothing is absorbed** — 'total' is meant literally.

3. **Diamonds** sparkle because their critical angle is only $24°$, so light entering is trapped and bounces many times before escaping.

questions.q: Explain thermal expansion in terms of particles, and give two useful applications and two problems it causes.
questions.solution:
**The explanation.** Heating gives particles more kinetic energy, so they vibrate more vigorously and push their neighbours slightly further away. The average spacing increases, and the object expands.

The particles themselves do **not** get bigger — only the gaps between them.

**Gases expand most** (particles almost free), then liquids, then solids (particles most tightly bound).

**Useful applications.**

1. **Liquid-in-glass thermometers** — mercury or alcohol expands up a narrow tube, and the narrowness magnifies a small expansion into a visible movement.

2. **Bimetallic strips** — brass and iron riveted together expand by different amounts, so the strip bends on heating. Used in thermostats and fire alarms.

3. **Riveting and shrink-fitting** — a hot metal tyre is fitted to a wheel and grips tightly as it cools.

**Problems.**

1. **Railway lines** buckle in hot weather, so expansion gaps are left between rails.

2. **Bridges and pipelines** need roller bearings or expansion loops, or they tear their own supports apart.

**Water is the great exception.** Between $0$°C and $4$°C it **contracts** on heating, and ice is **less dense** than water — which is why ice floats, why ponds freeze from the top down, and why fish survive the winter.

questions.q: Describe how sound is produced and transmitted, explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum, and describe how an echo can be used to measure distance.
questions.solution:
**Production.** A vibrating object — a string, a drum skin, vocal cords — pushes the air next to it back and forth, creating alternate **compressions** (crowded particles) and **rarefactions** (spread out).

**Transmission.** These pass outward as a **longitudinal wave**, each layer of air pushing the next. The air itself does not travel with the sound; it only vibrates about its position.

**Why not through a vacuum.** Sound needs **particles to compress**. A vacuum has none, so there is nothing to carry the disturbance.

**The bell jar experiment** shows it: an electric bell inside a jar grows fainter and fainter as the air is pumped out, until the hammer can be seen striking in complete silence. Light still passes, because electromagnetic waves need no medium.

**Speed.** About $340$ m/s in air, faster in liquids, and faster still in solids — roughly $5000$ m/s in steel — because the particles are closer and pass the disturbance on more quickly. This is the **opposite** of light.

**Echoes and distance.** A pulse is sent out, and the time $t$ for its return is measured:

$\text{distance} = \dfrac{v \times t}{2}$

The **halving** is essential — the sound has travelled there **and back**.

This is how **sonar** measures the depth of the sea, how **ultrasound** images an unborn child, and how a bat navigates in complete darkness.
